newsitem.title: USA: Dlr overcomes stock drop to end a tad higher in US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr overcomes stock drop to end a tad higher in US.

text.p: The dollar benefitted from a late afternoon short squeeze on Monday, rebounding from sharp early losses against the mark and other European currencies to end modestly higher.

The greenback had traded tick for tick with stocks for much of the session, dipping to its lowest level against the mark in roughly seven weeks as the Dow Industrials tumbled well over 100 points in early trade.
But when stocks began a fleeting recovery in the early afternoon, the dollar moved decisively up from its lows and kept climbing, even as the stock rebound faltered.
"It was basically a liquidity squeeze," said Robert Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets. "The market got caught, nobody had dollars left and everybody tried to square up."
The dollar ended the session at 1.6760/65 marks, up from 1.6733/38 at the open, and a seven-week low of 1.6615 marks touched in early dealings.
Against the yen, the dollar held steady for much of the U.S. session, popping higher in late trade to end at 123.75/80 against 123.57/62 at the open.
The dollar began the day on the defensive, piercing key support at 1.6680 marks and triggering stop-loss sell orders which took the rate down to its lows of the day.
Dealers said the impetus for the dollar's retreat was stocks, which tumbled in early trade on heightened concern aboutthe outlook for U.S. interest rates.

"The stock market weighed on the dollar very heavily," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole. "I think everybody was expecting more stock market weakness and we got it."

A series of economic releases -- including personal income and consumption data and the Chicago Purchasing Managers' manufacturing index -- showed ample strength in the U.S. economy, lending further credence to the view that the Federal Reserve could push official interest rates higher in the months ahead.
The Commerce Department reported that U.S. incomes jumped 0.9 percent to a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of $6.71 trillion in February -- the fastest rate of increase in eight months.

"The expectations of higher rates are not necessarily positive for the dollar right now because of their impact on the asset markets, in particular the stock market," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
The Dow Industrials ended the day down 157 points at 6583 -- unofficially the sixth largest drop in point terms.

In contrast to its performance against the mark, the dollar was consistently well-bid against the yen, benefitting from mark/yen strength and expectations of Japanese flows back into dollar-denominated assets in the new fiscal year.
Mark/yen popped above the 74 threshold for the first time since mid-February, before ending around 73.85.
Traders said the Easter holiday, which kept foreign exchange desks closed throughout much of Europe, may have been partly responsible for Monday's roller-coaster price fluctuations.
"The volumes were not normal and as such movement may have been exaggerated," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar ended modestly firmer at 1.4480/90 Swiss francs, up from 1.4465/75 at the open.
The British pound rose slightly to $1.6380/90 from $1.6372/82, while the Australian dollar inched higher to close at $0.7857/62 from $0.7853/58.
The dollar rose to near two-year highs against the Canadian dollar, ending at C$1.3839/44 from C$1.3803/08 in early dealings.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
